newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE - BP in quest for sweeter Colombian oil terms.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - BP in quest for sweeter Colombian oil terms.

text.p: British Petroleum Co Plc is the undisputed heavyweight when it comes to foreign investment in Colombia, but it has been slugging it out with the government for three years now and no winner has emerged as yet.

Colombia, the Latin American country where oil production is growing the fastest, would seem a top choice to look for investment opportunities because of its estimated 15 to 20 billion barrels of proven and estimated reserves.
But its attractiveness is limited by more than just frequent leftist guerrilla attacks on the country's oil infrastructure, as BP executives have learned only too well.
BP, a partner in the massive Cusiana and Cupiagua oil fields, is the single largest foreign investor in Colombia through its local subsidiary, BP Exploration Company (Colombia) Ltd.

But that has given it little apparent leverage in the talks it initiated in 1993 aimed at sweetening the terms of its contract to exploit the oil-rich Piedemonte field in Colombia's eastern plains, near Cusiana and Cupiagua.

Under the current so-called "sliding scale" terms of the contract, profits from the field are divided equally between BP and the state oil company Ecopetrol when total production is less than 60 million barrels. But Ecopetrol's share rises gradually as production increases, topping out at 76 percent when it reaches 150 million barrels.

BP spokesmen are reluctant to explain why they signed the contract in the first place, since they say it cuts their profit margin to no more than about eight to 12 percent over the life of the contract, well below the internationally accepted benchmark of 15 to 20 percent.
"The rate of return for BP is not anywhere near the rate of return that we would see as competitive in the international oil industry," said a company spokesman.
"The partnership needs to be readjusted," he told Reuters. "The gross economics of these fields is world class, it's just the way it's shared which is the problem."

The negatives for BP in Piedemonte, which contains anywhere from 600 million to one billion barrels of crude oil and condensates and 10 trillion cubic feet of gas, include extremely high drilling costs because of the depth of its oil reservoirs, which average between 15,000 and 18,000 feet (4,575 to 5,500 metres).

The spokesman said that even with a change in the Piedemonte contract, "Colombia will get more than 75 percent or even 80 percent of the value" of the field. He also noted that BP's share is eroded by oil royalties of 20 percent, a so-called war tax totalling $1.25 per barrel and a future remittance tax of seven percent on any profits transferred abroad.
BP and other foreign companies operating in Colombia also routinely pay the government for military protection of oil fields and pipelines.

At the end of the day, BP might have been better off putting the more than $440 million it has sunk into developing Piedemonte so far into U.S. Treasury bonds, given the low rate of return, the spokesman said.

However, reasonable it may seem to outsiders, BP's request for a bigger slice of Colombia's jealously-guarded oil pie has prompted a public outcry from leftist guerrillas and leaders of the country's powerful oil workers union, who have long opposed foreign investment in the industry.

The request has also drawn fire from Colombia's comptroller general and from at least one veteran member of Ecopetrol's board of directors, who stepped down earlier this month citing undue pressure from BP to change the contract.

President Ernesto Samper is widely believed to favour improving the contract terms for BP and he was quoted by one Western diplomat as saying that if necessary he would replace all 10 members of Ecopetrol's board -- minus one who was kidnapped by suspected guerrillas earlier this year -- to get the job done.

Samper has been severely weakened by his alleged ties to drug lords, however, and the oil workers union has raised the threat of a nationwide strike if he bows to what its populist leaders describe as the excessive demands of a greedy multinational.

Underscoring Samper's weakness, Interior Minister Horacio Serpa said last month the government would be willing to open talks with guerrillas on demands for the nationalisation of the oil industry as part of negotiations to end their long-running campaign of kidnappings and attacks on oil and coal projects.

That was before guerrillas launched a nationwide offensive in which hundreds of people have been killed -- pre-empting rebel calls for talks on the future of the oil industry -- but any decision on upgrading the BP contract could be a long time coming.
"There cannot be a deadline on this issue, and we're not threatening a deadline," the BP spokesman said.

He strongly denied accusations that the company had sought to take advantage of any perceived political weakness to win better contract terms but added that BP, which has successfully renegotiated contracts in Britain, Alaska, Norway, Vietnam and Venezuela in the past, could not continue throwing good money after bad forever.
